summary:
On longduration missions, astronauts must detect changes in their own health far from Earth. İstikbal Göklerdedir ("The Future Is in the Skies") is a local, privacy preserving health monitoring assistant that helps them do this. It tracks 74 indicators across bone, cardiovascular, immune, eye/brain (SANS), muscle, radiation and behavioral health. Each new value is compared with the astronaut's own pre-flight baseline and with the trajectory expected from published ISS cohorts, and a transparent rule-based engine flags risks with concrete actions the crew can take on board.

Its key idea is operational realism. On launch the app asks "Are you in space or on Earth?" In space mode it asks only for the 27 measurements possible with equipment NASA keeps aboard the ISS, such as ECG, blood pressure, ultrasound, OCT, body-mass measurement, actigraphy and the Cognition test battery. It never asks for MRI or DXA, which do not exist on board; it estimates them from the model instead. A local AI assistant, grounded in PubMed and NASA NTRS papers that it downloads automatically, answers questions and writes personal risk reports that are saved for later review.
details:
What it does. İstikbal Göklerdedir lets an astronaut, or a flight surgeon on the ground, record health indicators, see how they compare with what is expected, and get clear warnings with actions. It covers the challenge's four areas — immune changes, bone loss, cardiovascular events and behavioral health — plus SANS, muscle, radiation and sensorimotor changes, in 74 parameters.

How it works.

1. Space or Earth mode. The first screen asks where the user is. On Earth (pre or post flight) all 74 parameters can be entered, including DXA, QCT, HR-pQCT, MRI, tilt/LBNP and clinical neurophysiology. In space only 27 parameters are offered, each linked to equipment NASA keeps aboard the ISS: the CHeCS ECG and blood-pressure unit and tonometer, ISS ultrasound (heart, carotid, optic-nerve sheath), OCT, SLAMMD/BMMD body mass, CEVIS + PPFS for VO2, ESA's MARES dynamometer, dosimeters, wrist actigraphy, questionnaires and the NASA Cognition battery. Point-of-care blood counts (HemoCue WBC DIFF, rHEALTH ONE) are offered and labelled experimental. Lab results from samples returned to Earth can optionally be entered, but this is off by default because a Mars crew may not have that route.

2. Personal baseline and literature model. Every parameter has a reference range, an expected 180 day change and a recovery half-life taken from ISS cohorts with ARED exercise. Each new value is compared with the astronaut's own baseline and the expected value for that flight day. A personal multiplier increases predicted bone loss when pre-flight bone turnover is high.

3. Estimates for what cannot be measured in space. In space mode the dashboard shows a model estimate of today's value for parameters such as femoral-neck BMD, marked as an estimate to confirm after landing.

4. Transparent risk engine. Rules flag bone loss and fracture, renal stones, orthostatic intolerance, SANS, radiation, deconditioning, immune dysregulation with latent-virus reactivation (VZV, EBV, CMV), and sleep deficiency and behavioral health. Thresholds are published clinical cut-offs, for example sleep ≥ 7 h, PSQI > 5, PHQ-9 ≥ 10, ANC < 1.5 and ALC < 1.0 ×10³/µL. The few thresholds not defined in the literature are labelled "project heuristic" on screen. Behavioral outputs are screening results, not diagnoses. An instant rule-based report can be generated in a second, without any AI.

5. Self-updating AI assistant. A local language model (Llama 3.1 via Ollama) answers questions by text or voice and writes personal risk reports, which are saved in a report history. In space mode it asks only for measurements possible on board. At start-up the app downloads new space-medicine papers from PubMed and NASA NTRS, so answers cite current research even when the model is older.

Benefits. The astronaut gets early, personal and explainable warnings without waiting for the ground, which matters on missions with communication delays. Data never leave the computer. Every number and threshold names its source.

What we hope to achieve. A tool that helps crews act on early signs on Artemis and Mars missions, and that could be validated with real flight data and flight surgeons. The same approach could support remote patient monitoring on Earth.

Example case. The repository includes a fictional 180-day ISS case ("Astronaut K", 507 measurements) consistent with published cohorts. It shows high bone turnover, hypercalciuria, an increase in optic-nerve-sheath diameter, orthostatic heart-rate rise at landing, asymptomatic VZV shedding, in-flight sleep under 6 h, and a normal depression screen.

Tools and languages. Python 3.12, Streamlit, SQLite, pandas, NumPy, Plotly, pypdf, openpyxl, Pillow; Ollama (Llama 3.1, LLaVA) with optional OpenAI-compatible or Anthropic APIs; NCBI E-utilities and the NASA NTRS API; DuckDuckGo search. The user interface, documentation and reference list are in English; the AI assistant also answers in Turkish when asked in Turkish.

Why the name. "İstikbal Göklerdedir" ("The future is in the skies") is a well-known saying of our great leader Mustafa Kemal Atatürk, founder of the Republic of Türkiye, encouraging the country to invest in aviation.
